OPINIONS AND BASIS THEREOF It is my opinion that the supply, marketing, distribution, and sale of OPMS Kratom fails to comply with basic industry and regulatory standards of care for supplements, and in particular New Dietary Ingredients (NDI). The Kratom at issue in this case was misbranded under the industry and regulatory standards that Page 6

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 8 of 31 govern health claims, labeling, and branding for dietary ingredients and supplements. Defendants violated the standards that prohibit the marketing, distribution, and sale of unapproved and new drugs. My testimony and the conclusions reached in this report are and will be based on my education, training, and experience. A. OPMS Kratom: A New Dietary Ingredient Not Safe for Human Consumption. In the supplement industry, any entity looking to sell an ingredient or supplement for human consumption should first become familiar with the standards that govern the substance that is proposed for sale, including any agency guidance provided on the status of that substance. Kratom is a “New Dietary Ingredient” (NDI) for purposes of the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA). The FDA’s classification of kratom as an NDI is based upon the definitions established by Congress in DSHEA and is well publicized. See, for example, Import Alert 54-15 (FDA, 04/08/2021). The FDA has already established that kratom is an NDI. According to the publicly available Import Alert, to the best of the FDA’s knowledge, there is no information demonstrating that this substance was marketed as a dietary ingredient in the United States before October 15, 1994. See, Import Alert 54-15; see also, FDA letter to American Botanicals Corporation, dated Nov. 5, 2021. Because kratom is an NDI, any manufacturer or distributor proposing to sell kratom for human consumption should first familiarize themselves with the industry practices and standards that are necessary to confirm that the product is Page 7

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 31 reasonably expected to be safe. This standard of due diligence is also necessary for the premarket “NDI Notification” which must be submitted to the FDA at least 75 days before kratom can be introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce. Under this standard, the entity must substantiate a history of use or other evidence of safety establishing that the dietary ingredient, when used under the conditions recommended or suggested in the labeling of the dietary supplement, will be reasonably be expected to be safe. If the required premarket NDI Notification does not acceptably demonstrate appropriate safety, then any dietary supplement product containing kratom is classified as an adulterated product, and not appropriate for sale to consumers because its safety has not been established. Based on the information provided, none of the named defendants ever verified that the OPMS kratom products manufactured and sold by them were reasonably safe for human consumption, either before or after they were marketed. FDA Response Letters to NDI Notifications pertaining to kratom uniformly confirm that the safety of kratom and its derivatives has not been established, and these products are not reasonably expected to be safe. Publicly available information from the FDA and elsewhere identify serious concerns regarding the toxicity of kratom in multiple organ systems, with risks to humans that include the risk of death. Even Dr. Henningfield, who has worked directly with Mr. Peyton Palaio regarding kratom, testified that it was in the public interest for the OPMS product line to meet the safety standards required for an acceptable NDIN. See, Henningfield Dep. at pp.86 & 96-97. It is a clear violation of industry standard for any manufacturer or Page 8

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 31 distributor to sell a product for human consumption that has been publicly declared by the FDA to be adulterated because of inadequate information regarding its safety for consumers. B. OPMS Kratom: Misbranded and Sold as an Unapproved, New Drug. In addition to being an adulterated NDI, OPMS Kratom was misbranded and sold as an unapproved new drug, without adequate warnings. Kratom, kratom- containing dietary supplements, and bulk dietary ingredients are subject to important industry standards and regulations that prohibit the sale of products that are “misbranded”, “drugs”, and/or “new drugs”. See, e.g., 21 CFR § 101.93(f) and (g). These standards focus on the intended use of the products; the labeling, marketing, and/or promotion of such products; and the types of claims made about the products. These standards have been the subject of well publicized enforcement actions by the DOJ, including a Final Debarment Order and federal court decrees. See, Matthew Dailey: Final Debarment Order, FDA-2019-N-3310, Federal Register Vol. 85, No. 52, page 15193-4 (March 17, 2020); US DOJ Press Release: Michigan Man Sentenced for Unlawfully Importing and Distributing Misbranded Drugs (May 8, 2019); US DOJ Press Release: North Carolina Man Ran Lucrative Fraud Scheme Selling Unapproved Substances that Mimic the Health Benefits of Legal Drugs (August 31, 2021); Consent Decree of Condemnation, Destruction, and Permanent Injunction, United States v. 577 Cartons, CV 14-5729 PA (MRWx) (U.S.D.C., CA C.D., W.D., Dec. 1, 2014); Consent Decree of Condemnation and Destruction, USA vs. Defendant Articles (USDC FL, October 26, 2021); FDA Page 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 11 of 31 Announces Seizure of Adulterated Dietary Supplements Containing Kratom (FDA News Release, and federal order, dated October 26, 2021); see also, FDA and Kratom (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/public-health-focus/fda-and-kratom) and FDA Warns Consumers Not to Use OPMS Black Liquid Kratom (July 26, 2024; https://www.fda.gov/food/alerts-advisories-safety-information/fda-warns- consumers-not-use-optimized-plant-mediated-solutions-opms-black-liquid-kratom). 1. Kratom should not be sold as a drug. This standard is violated when kratom is sold for the purpose of treating and mitigating diseases, including but not limited to addiction, and to otherwise affect the structure and function of the human body. Knowingly selling kratom for its drug effects is also improper. For years, FDA Warning Letters have been publicly available as industry guidance, reinforcing the obligation to avoid selling kratom as a drug or otherwise. See, for example, DHHS NDIN Response Letter re: Luke Dodd, “Atomic K” (September 22, 2015); FDA warning letter to “Cali Botanicals, LLC” (Warning Letter 57320, June 11, 2019). 2. Kratom should not be sold as a “new drug”. The FDA Warning letters also address the industry standard against the sale of kratom as a “new drug”. The standard prohibiting sale of unapproved “new drugs” is violated when kratom, which it is not generally recognized as safe and effective, and for which it has not been approved based on scientific data submitted by a drug sponsor to demonstrate that the drug is safe and effective, is sold for human consumption under the direction of a healthcare professional. See, 21 U.S.C. § 321 Page 10

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 12 of 31 (p). The requirement that kratom first be approved by the FDA before it is sold as a new drug is designed to ensure the health and safety of consumers, like Harmony Moller. According to industry guidance, there are currently no FDA-approved kratom drug products. 3. Kratom should not be sold as a “misbranded” drug or sold without adequate directions for use. A kratom product is “misbranded” when: (1) it is knowingly sold for use as a drug but fails to bear adequate directions for its intended uses; and/or (2) it is knowingly offered for conditions that are not amenable to self-diagnosis and treatment by persons who are not medical practitioners. In such cases, adequate directions for the intended uses cannot be written to allow safe use by the ordinary consumer. See, 21 USC § 352(f)(1); 352(a), (f), (i), (o) (identifying misbranded drugs); see also, FDA Warning letter to Umbrella (May 18, 2021). The Consumer Product Safety Commission notes that consumers will assume a product is safe based on the labeling. It is a violation of the industry standard to sell kratom intended for use as a drug, without labeling bearing adequate directions for use, warnings and cautions for safe use, and other “material information” necessary for proper use of the product. 21 CFR § 1.21; 21 CFR § 101.9(k) (labeling a supplement as effective in regard to a disease or symptom is misbranding); and 21 CFR § 201.5 (adequate directions for use defined); 21 CFR § 352(a), (f), (i), (o) (misbranding via false and misleading labels). The OPMS Kratom products at issue were sold in violation of these standards. The OPMS defendants have testified to knowingly selling OPMS kratom products Page 11

The warning on the OPMS kratom packages say nothing about seizure, cardiorespiratory adverse effects, or death but is instead a caution for those who “ARE PREGNANT, PLAN TO BECOME PREGNANT, OR WHILE BREASTFEEDING”. A properly prepared NDIN would have needed to address and warn about these basic issues of human safety, such as maximum safe dose, and risks of addiction, seizure, cardiorespiratory adverse effects, and death. Kratom containing products must not be promoted or sold for health and medically related purposes, without first complying with the safeguards, procedures, and approvals for promoting such products for medicinal or drug purposes. Yet, the facts of this case show that OPMS Kratom products were sold for those purposes. Despite recognizing that these products were not to be marketed as a substitute for medical treatment, Mr. Gabbay, Mr. Reilly, and Mr. Palaio, individually and through their corporate entities intended that the products be sold for that very purpose and knew that OPMS consumers were in fact using it for that purpose. October 16, 2025, Deposition of JOpen, LLC at pp.65:15-66:15; October 28, 2024, Deposition of Martian Sales at pp.206:23-207:10; October 9, 2025, Deposition of Peyton Palaio at pp. 44:11-45:19. OPMS kratom consumers, including Harmony Moller, were not properly warned of the serious risks from Kratom, including the risks of seizures, cardiorespiratory adverse effects, death, dependence and addiction, and drug-drug interactions. These risks are identified in FDA guidance and the related peer- reviewed scientific and medical literature. See, e.g., Xiaotong Li, et al, An evaluation of adverse drug reactions and outcomes attributed to kratom in the US FDAERS system 2004 to 2021 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10264943/). The OPMS kratom warning that it is “only for use as a botanical specimen” is disingenuous at best. This does not make the product legal and does not allow a business to avoid the testing and approvals necessary to ensure that products containing kratom are safe for human consumption before they are put on the shelf. Healthcare professionals are frequently unfamiliar with non-prescription botanicals like kratom. And it is false to suggest that medical professionals will instruct on the “safe” use of a OPMS product that was never verified as safe for human consumption in the first place. This generic warning is also incomplete and deceptive in failing to communicate the severe nature of the dangers documented for kratom, which includes the risk of seizure, cardiorespiratory adverse effects, addiction, and death. The OPMS labeling does not provide directions for use that might have mitigated these serious risks. There is no maximum safe dose specified, or any dose at all. There is no indication that a maximum safe dose has ever been established for OPMS kratom via NDIN, or any other process. These violations of industry and regulatory standards related to warnings and directions are very serious, as Kratom consumers may forego necessary medical treatments and supervision without any information to guide them in the safe use of a product improperly sold as an alternative to medical care. D. OPMS Labeling Failed To Identify The Entity Responsible For The Product, Rendering OPMS Kratom Misbranded. Name and Place of Business. The OPMS label is deemed misbranded because it does not correctly identify the actual name and place of business for the entity responsible for the product. FDA Guidance, at Q&A No. 1, citing Section 403(e) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. § 343(e)); see also, Warning Letter to Big Easy Page 14

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 16 of 31 Confections, LLC, dated August 14, 2014. The label shall include the name and place of business, including the city, state, and zip code unless the address is listed in a current city directory or telephone directory. 21 CFR § 101.5(d). The OPMS label identifies Choice Organics, and provides a phone number, address, and email. However, Choice Organics is an entity made up out of whole cloth in response to a Utah state enforcement action. Further, the address, phone number, and email have had periods in which they have not functioned. Not to mention, the information simply does not accurately or honestly identify the entity or entities responsible for OPMS kratom. See Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 42 to Plaintiff’s Memorandum in Support of Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (Dkt. No. 132). Mr. Gabbay testified that he was familiar with this requirement, and that he was previously informed that his kratom products were being destroyed for the failure to disclose such information. However, rather than provide an honest disclosure, Mr. Gabbay’s response was to invent names for businesses that did not exist (“Choice Organics” for OPMS and “KonoLabs” for Whole Herbs), and identify California post office boxes as the place of business, even though an actual street address is to be included and no business is conducted in those locations. March 14, 2025, Deposition of JOpen, LLC (Rachel McKibban v JOpen, LLC, et al.) at pp.66:8-68:24, pp.79:19-81:3, pp.212:15-213:5, pp.219:17-220:4, & pp.239:24-240:20. This deceptive marketing ploy, including the listing of Choice Organics on the OPMS kratom website, is inconsistent with the basic standards for transparency about who is responsible for Page 15

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 17 of 31 products consumed by humans. The marketing ploy is likely to mislead many consumers. Adverse Event Reporting. As with the fictional OPMS labeling, the adverse event reporting system for OPMS kratom presents a disturbing lack of regard for the industry standards and human safety. The FDA’s labeling guidance, which is based on federal law, makes clear that the label must enable consumers to report serious adverse events to the actual place of business, via the domestic address or phone number. FDA Guidance for Industry: Q&A Regarding Labeling of Dietary Supplements (Federal Register Vol. 74, No. 168, p. 45221; Docket Number FDA-2007-D-0209; September 2009); see for example, Warning Letter to Big Easy Confections, LLC, dated August 14, 2014. The OPMS label is deemed misbranded because it does not specify a complete domestic address or domestic phone number through which the responsible person may receive a report of a serious adverse event. FDA Guidance, at Q&A No. 1, citing Section 403(y) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. § 343(y)). This is a basic directive to provide “all information necessary to enable a serious adverse event report to reach the responsible person.” Id. The FDA also recommends “a clear, prominent statement” informing consumers that they may report serious adverse events via the address or phone. Id. Q&A No. 2. The FDA guidance also emphasizes that the responsible person must use product labeling that includes information on how to report an adverse event, must maintain an established system for collecting adverse event reports, and must Page 16

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 241-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 18 of 31 submit serious adverse event reports to FDA no later than 15 business days after a report is received. 21 USC § 379aa-1(c)(1)-(2); see FDA Warning Letter to Market America Inc. (MARCS-CMS 588959 – Feb. 12, 2020) (warning for failure to report adverse events); FDA Warning Letter to BHP Holdings Inc., dba BioPure Healing Products (MARCS-CMS 597687 – June 17, 2020) (manufacturer improperly rejected adverse event complaints as “invalid” without proper investigation and assessment of product safety risk). Prompt submission of serious adverse event reports is important for public health reasons. A properly functioning adverse event reporting system is an important feature of product and consumer safety. Both the FDA and the manufacturer must be aware of the extent to which a particular product may be harming or killing consumers. The information identifies dangers and trends and allows those responsible to prevent future harms through recalls, enforcement actions, improved design and warnings, or other actions. Notwithstanding the importance of effective adverse event reporting, Defendants did not have a set of procedures in place for assessing the seriousness of an adverse report, gathering the necessary information, and ensuring it is properly handled until approximately early 2025. October 16, 2025, Deposition of JOpen, LLC at pp.34:22-36:3, pp.76:25-77:22, pp.124:17-128:2, & pp.159:13-159:23; October 28, 2024, Deposition of Martian Sales, Inc. at pp.119:3-120:13 & pp.258:23- 259:1-5. See, FDA Human Foods - Guidance Document, Guidance for Industry: Questions and Answers Regarding Adverse Event Reporting and Recordkeeping for Page 17

Kratom Is Not a Food. I understand that those responsible for OPMS may claim that they may disregard the foregoing safety standards because kratom is a “food”. Based on my review, OPMS was never intended to be sold as a “food” and cannot be credibly identified as a “food”. See, 21 U.S.C. § 321(ff)(2)(B) (supplements should not be represented for use as a conventional food or as a sole item of a meal or the diet); FDA – Questions and Answers on Dietary Supplements (2/21/24) (https://www.fda.gov/food/information-consumers-using- dietary-supplements/questions-and-answers-dietary-supplements). A theory that OPMS is a “food” is contradicted by the labeling, the intended use, and the way the product has been designed, marketed, and distributed. There is no statement of identity to credibly suggest that OPMS is a food. Food products generally do not direct the consumer to inform their physician of the “alkaloid content” of the material before consuming it. Food product labels do not instruct a consumer that the leafy material is to be used as a “botanical specimen”. Even if a kratom product were characterized and labeled as “food”, it would still need to be safe for human consumption. In fact, the safety standard for food ingredients places a higher burden on the industry than the standard for dietary ingredients in supplements. See, FDA – How U.S. FDA’s GRAS Notification Program Works (2/9/18) (https://www.fda.gov/food/generally-recognized-safe- gras/how-us-fdas-gras-notification-program-works). The GRAS standard Page 20

Even an agricultural food product needs to be safe for its intended use when put on the market. There is no evidence that American consumers are sitting down for a bowl of kratom as a meal or otherwise consuming the kratom as a food. E.
